Series::is_signed¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

bool Series::is_signed() const

What It Does¶

Returns true when the Series’ dtype can represent negative values — signed integers (Int8 … Int64), all real floating formats, and both complex formats — and false for the unsigned integers (UInt8 … UInt64) and Bool.

It is a dtype test, not a value test: it reports whether the format has a sign, not whether the current data contains a negative number. A signed Int32 tensor holding only positive values is still is_signed() == true; an unsigned UInt8 tensor is is_signed() == false even if every value is 0.

The reason to care is that arithmetic on an unsigned dtype wraps instead of going negative. neg(), sub(), and anything that can produce a value below zero silently roll around modulo 2^bits on an unsigned Series. is_signed() is the guard that says “this subtraction is safe to interpret literally” — where it returns false, a result near zero may actually be a huge positive number.

Across every scalar type, the three category predicates behave as:

dtype

is_complex

is_floating_point

is_signed

Bool

false

false

false

UInt8 … UInt64

false

false

false

Int8 … Int64

false

false

true

Float16, BFloat16, Float32, Float64, the 8-bit floats

false

true

true

Complex64, Complex128

true

false

true

Note Bool and the unsigned integers land in the same false column for is_signed(), but for different reasons — Bool has no numeric sign concept at all, the unsigned integers deliberately trade the sign bit for range.

Parameters¶

None.

Returns¶

bool true for signed integer, real floating, and complex dtypes; false for unsigned integer and Bool.

Gradient¶

Not applicable — is_signed() returns a plain bool.

Examples¶

Example 1. Signed integers, floats, and complex answer true; unsigned integers and Bool answer false.

for (auto st : {pluss::ScalarType::Bool, pluss::ScalarType::UInt8,
                pluss::ScalarType::UInt64, pluss::ScalarType::Int8,
                pluss::ScalarType::Int64, pluss::ScalarType::Float32,
                pluss::ScalarType::Complex64}) {
  auto x = pluss::series::zeros({1}, st);
  std::cout << x.dtype() << " -> is_signed=" << std::boolalpha
            << x.is_signed() << "\n";
}

Output¶

bool -> is_signed=false
uint8 -> is_signed=false
uint64 -> is_signed=false
int8 -> is_signed=true
int64 -> is_signed=true
float32 -> is_signed=true
complex64 -> is_signed=true

Example 2. neg() on an unsigned Series wraps around — this is the hazard is_signed() == false is warning about.

auto u = pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}).to(pluss::ScalarType::UInt8);
std::cout << "u.is_signed()=" << std::boolalpha << u.is_signed() << "\n";
pluss::series::print(std::cout, u.neg());

Output¶

u.is_signed()=false
Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=uint8, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[255, 254, 253]

-1 in UInt8 is 255, -2 is 254, and so on — two’s-complement wraparound. On a signed dtype the same call would give [-1, -2, -3].

Example 3. Subtraction that would go negative underflow-wraps on an unsigned dtype.

auto a = pluss::make_series({0, 1, 2}).to(pluss::ScalarType::UInt8);
auto b = pluss::make_series({1, 1, 1}).to(pluss::ScalarType::UInt8);
std::cout << "a.is_signed()=" << std::boolalpha << a.is_signed() << "\n";
pluss::series::print(std::cout, a.sub(b));

Output¶

a.is_signed()=false
Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=uint8, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[255, 0, 1]

0 - 1 becomes 255, not -1. If differences can be negative, convert to a signed dtype first (a.to(ScalarType::Int32).sub(...)), or check is_signed() and branch.

Example 4. is_signed() is a dtype question; signbit is the per-element one.

auto x = pluss::make_series({-2.0, 0.0, 3.0});
std::cout << "x.is_signed()=" << std::boolalpha << x.is_signed()
          << " (the dtype can hold negatives)\n";
pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.signbit());

Output¶

x.is_signed()=true (the dtype can hold negatives)
Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=bool, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[true, false, false]

is_signed() is one bool for the whole tensor — “could any value be negative”; signbit is one bool per element — “is this value negative” (and it catches -0.0, which compares equal to 0).

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • is_signed() == false covers two dtypes with different rationales: the unsigned integers (range-for-sign trade) and Bool (no numeric sign at all).

  • On an unsigned Series, neg(), sub(), and any op that can dip below zero wrap modulo 2^bits — a “small” result can be a huge positive number. Convert to a signed dtype before such arithmetic if negatives are meaningful.

  • The answer is about the format, not the data. A signed tensor of all- positive values is still is_signed() == true.

  • For the elementwise “is this value negative” question use signbit, which also distinguishes -0.0 from 0.0.

Summary¶

is_signed() reports whether the dtype can represent negatives:

  • true for signed integers, all real floats, and complex

  • false for unsigned integers and Bool

  • format-only — a signed tensor of positives is still true

  • the guard before subtraction / negation whose result could go below zero on an unsigned dtype (where it wraps)

  • Series::is_complex / Series::is_floating_point: the other two category predicates.

  • Series::signbit: the per-element “is this value negative” question, -0.0-aware.

  • Series::to: convert to a signed dtype before sign-sensitive arithmetic.
